description.content:
Captures the canonical snapshot of the draft, including the data dictionary definitions
it was written against, stores its SHA-256 checksum, and moves the version to
`PENDING_APPROVAL`. After this nothing about the version changes: edits and a second
submit are 409 `POLICY_VERSION_FROZEN`. No request body.
Before freezing, the full policy validation of `POST .../validate` runs (SYSTEM_DESIGN.md
9.3): completeness (a scorecard, a decision matrix, and at least one required test case),
the RAC rules, the scorecard, the decision matrix against the scorecard range, and the test
cases, all against the dictionary version the draft is pinned to. If any check fails, the
answer is a 422 `POLICY_VALIDATION_FAILED` listing every problem (paths start with
`scorecard.` or `decision_matrix.` for those sections) and the draft stays a DRAFT.
When those checks pass, every test case is also **executed** through the decision
pipeline (RF-013): a required case whose decision, grade (when it names one), or reason
codes differ from the actual result is a validation issue
(`decision_mismatch`, `grade_mismatch`, `reason_codes_mismatch`, `input_rejected`,
`validation_error_not_raised`, `evaluation_failed`) and the submit is refused. Optional
cases that fail do not block.

**Approval request (RF-019).** In the same transaction the submit opens an approval
request that pins the policy version, its checksum, and the **current version of the
approval workflow** of the product and policy scope (`GET /approval-workflows`). The
response is the frozen version plus `approval_request`, in the shape of
`GET /approval-requests/{request_id}`, with step 1 active. A product and scope without a
workflow cannot be submitted: `409 APPROVAL_WORKFLOW_NOT_CONFIGURED`, and the draft stays a
DRAFT. Approvers act with `POST /approval-requests/{request_id}/actions`; the final
approval publishes the version atomically (RF-020).

item.name: Replace the scorecard of a draft

request.name: Replace the scorecard of a draft

description.content:
Replaces the whole scorecard in one step: `total_score = base_score + the points of the one
bin each characteristic selects` (SYSTEM_DESIGN.md 10.3). Characteristics keep the order
given, and each one scores one numeric data dictionary variable.

**Bins are half-open intervals `[min_value, max_value)`**: `min_value` is included,
`max_value` is not. An omitted or null `min_value` means no lower limit and an omitted or
null `max_value` means no upper limit. Bins are listed in ascending order and must cover
every value the variable can have exactly once: the first bin starts at or below the
variable's dictionary minimum (or has no `min_value`), each bin starts where the previous
one ends (`gap` / `overlap` otherwise), and the last bin ends above the dictionary maximum
(or has no `max_value`). So every valid input selects exactly one bin. Bounds follow the
variable type: whole numbers for INTEGER (`must_be_integer`), at most the variable's scale
for DECIMAL (`exceeds_scale`). They are returned in shortest form (`"0.30"` becomes `"0.3"`).

`base_score`, `points`, and `missing_points` are decimal strings with at most two decimals
(NUMERIC(12,2)); they are returned with exactly two and may be negative. Sums are exact.
`missing_points` is the explicit outcome when the variable is absent or null, and is only
allowed for an optional input variable (`variable_always_present` otherwise).

Everything is checked against the dictionary version the draft is pinned to. Nothing is
stored unless the whole scorecard is valid; every problem is reported with its path
(`characteristics[1].bins[2].min_value`). Sending the scorecard the draft already has
changes nothing. Only a DRAFT can change (409 `POLICY_VERSION_FROZEN`).

changes. Submit runs the same checks and refuses the version (422

Checks: **completeness** (a scorecard, a decision matrix, and at least one required test
case: `missing_section`, `no_required_test_cases`; RAC rules are optional); every **RAC
expression** compiles and type-checks; the **scorecard** variables exist and are numeric
and its bins cover each variable exactly once; the **decision matrix** covers the
scorecard's score range; every **test case** references existing variables, grades, and
reason codes, and its input passes or fails the data dictionary as its expected outcome
says. Paths are those of the editing endpoints, prefixed `scorecard.` and
`decision_matrix.` for those sections.

**Golden tests (RF-013).** When no other check found a problem, every test case is
executed with the same code a decision uses: input validation, derived features (DSR and
net disposable income), RAC rules, scorecard, decision matrix, and precedence. The
result of each case is in `golden_tests.results` with the `actual` outcome and what
differs from the expectation (`mismatches`). The decision and the reason codes must
match (reason codes as a set: a case that lists none expects none), the grade only when
the case names one, and a case that expects `INPUT_VALIDATION_ERROR` must be refused.
A technical failure (`EVALUATION_ERROR`, `POLICY_CONFIGURATION_ERROR`) is never a pass.
A mismatch of a **required** case is an issue and makes `valid` false; a mismatch of an
optional case is reported but does not. If another check failed the cases are not run,
and `pending_checks` says so: a skipped check is always listed so it is never mistaken
for a pass. `pending_checks` is empty when everything ran.

item.description: Credit decisions against the active policy (RF-014).

request.name: Evaluate a loan application

description.content:
Runs a credit decision for one application against the **active policy** of its product
(SYSTEM_DESIGN.md 10, 13.2 to 13.4). The active version is resolved once at the start of
the request, so a publish during the request cannot change the version it uses, and the
response names that version (`policy_version`). The compiled policy comes from an
in-memory cache keyed by the version id and the checksum of its frozen snapshot (RF-016,
SYSTEM_DESIGN.md 10.6): every decision still reads which version is active, so a publish
takes effect on the next decision, and a retired product or a removed binding is seen at
once. The cache changes no request or response.

Pipeline: the applicant data is validated and normalized against the data dictionary the
policy was written for; the derived features are built (`dsr_ratio` and
`net_disposable_income`, exact, with the formula version); the RAC rules run in order;
unless a hard rule rejected the application, the scorecard selects one bin per
characteristic and adds its points, the decision matrix maps the total to a grade and a
decision, and the precedence hard RAC `REJECT` > matrix `REJECT` > soft RAC `REFER` >
matrix `APPROVE`/`REFER` gives `final_decision`.

**Applicant data.** Integers are JSON numbers, decimals (money, ratios) are **strings**
such as `"12000000.00"`; a JSON number for money is refused (`invalid_type`) instead of
being rounded. A decimal has at most 18 integer digits and 32 fraction digits and no
exponent; anything else is `invalid_type`. A missing or `null` required value, a wrong
type, a value outside the
dictionary range, too many decimals, a key that is not a dictionary variable
(`unknown_variable`), and a derived value sent by the caller (`derived_not_allowed`) are
all `422 INPUT_VALIDATION_ERROR`, listed together with paths such as
`applicant.monthly_income`. Invalid data is an error, never a `REJECT`.

**Errors are not decisions.** `409 POLICY_NOT_ACTIVE` when the product is retired or has
no active policy (a draft or a pending version is never evaluated); `404
PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND`; `500 POLICY_CONFIGURATION_ERROR` when the active policy cannot be
evaluated; `500 EVALUATION_ERROR` for a technical failure while evaluating. None of them
carries a decision, and the cause is logged server-side only.

**Stored once per `Idempotency-Key` (RF-015, SYSTEM_DESIGN.md 13.5).** The header is
required. The claim of the key, the evaluation, and the storing of the run and its rule
traces happen in one transaction, and the response is sent only after the commit. The
key is scoped to the caller (the authenticated user) and tied to a hash of the request:
- **Same key, same request** (key order and white space do not matter): the stored
  decision is returned, with the same `decision_id` and `created_at`, and the response
  header `Idempotent-Replayed: true`. Nothing is evaluated, and the active policy is not
  consulted, so a replay still works after the policy changed.
- **Same key, different request:** `409 IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT`.
- **A duplicate that arrives while the first request is still running** waits for it
  (bounded by the 3 second request limit) and returns its decision. There is never a
  second run for one key.
- **No decision, no stored key:** an invalid request, an unknown product, a product with
  no active policy, or a technical failure rolls back and leaves the key unused, so a
  corrected retry with the same key is evaluated.

A stored decision keeps the policy version and checksum it was made with, the normalized
input, and the full trace, and cannot be changed or deleted. Read it with
`GET /decisions/{decision_id}`. Any `API_CONSUMER` may evaluate any product;
per-product authorization needs API clients, which do not exist yet.
The request and response bodies of the decision endpoints are never written to the
activity log (they hold the applicant's financial data); the log keeps the caller, the
route, the status, the duration, and the request id.

item.name: Simulate an applicant against a policy version

request.name: Simulate an applicant against a policy version

description.content:
Evaluates one applicant against **any version**, draft or frozen, and returns the full
trace (SYSTEM_DESIGN.md 12, RF-017). It is the way to see what a draft does before it is
submitted. It uses **the same evaluation core as `POST /decisions/evaluate`**: input
validation against the data dictionary the version is pinned to, the derived features,
the RAC rules in order, the scorecard, the decision matrix, and the precedence. Given the
same content and the same applicant, a simulation returns the same `final_decision`,
`risk_grade`, `total_score`, `reason_codes`, and trace as a decision would.

**Nothing is written and nothing in production changes.** No decision run, rule trace, or
idempotency key is stored (so no `Idempotency-Key` is needed, and the same request can be
repeated), the active policy binding does not move, the version is not locked, edited, or
frozen, and the compiled policy cache of the Decision API is neither read nor filled. A
draft is evaluated from its content as saved at the moment of the request, so an edit is
visible on the next call. The response has no `decision_id`, `created_at`, or
`application_id`, and `stored` is `false`.

**Applicant data** follows the rules of `POST /decisions/evaluate`: integers are JSON
numbers, decimals are strings, derived variables must not be sent, and invalid data is
`422 INPUT_VALIDATION_ERROR` with every problem listed. It is never a `REJECT`.

**A version that cannot be evaluated yet.** A draft is often incomplete: no scorecard, a
decision matrix that does not cover the score range, or an expression that no longer
compiles. That is `422 POLICY_NOT_EVALUABLE`, whose `message` says what is missing. It is a
statement about the draft, not a decision about the applicant. The version is compiled
before the applicant is checked, so a version that cannot be evaluated is reported first.
A technical fault is `500 INTERNAL_ERROR`.

`policy_version.checksum` is `null` until the version is frozen. The body is the
applicant's financial data, so request and response bodies of this route are never
written to the activity log, as for the decision endpoints.

(`duplicate_name`). The product must exist and be ACTIVE (`unknown_product`,
`product_inactive`); `policy_scope` defaults to `DEFAULT`. A product and policy scope
have one workflow (`409 APPROVAL_WORKFLOW_CONFLICT`); change it with
`POST /approval-workflows/{workflow_id}/versions`.

append-only: a workflow, a version, and its steps are never edited or deleted (database
triggers refuse it). Audit events arrive with RF-022; until then `created_by` records

item.name: Approve or reject the active step

request.name: Approve or reject the active step

description.content:
The approval state machine (SYSTEM_DESIGN.md 11.2, 11.3). Only the **active step** of an
open request accepts actions. The approver's roles and approval scopes are read
server-side from the identity module; the body cannot claim a role. Checks, in order:

- the request is open (`409 APPROVAL_REQUEST_CLOSED`);
- `step`, if sent, is the active step (`409 APPROVAL_STEP_NOT_ACTIVE`);
- the caller is not the submitter (`403 SELF_APPROVAL_FORBIDDEN`), even with every role;
- the caller has not acted on this request before (`409 APPROVAL_ALREADY_GIVEN`): one
  person acts once per request, so one approver never satisfies two tiers and a quorum
  always counts distinct people;
- the caller holds the step's role and, if it names one, its scope
  (`403 APPROVER_NOT_ELIGIBLE`).

`REJECT` (with a `comment`) closes the request as `REJECTED` and the policy version
becomes `REJECTED`; the analyst revises by cloning it into a new draft. `APPROVE` counts
toward the step's quorum; when reached, the next step becomes active.

**The approval that completes the last step publishes (RF-020, SYSTEM_DESIGN.md 9.4).**
In one transaction: the action is stored, the request closes `APPROVED`, the version
(only if it still has the submitted checksum and its snapshot compiles) becomes
`APPROVED` and then `ACTIVE`, the previously active version of the policy becomes
`ARCHIVED`, the active binding moves to the new version, and an audit event
`POLICY_VERSION_PUBLISHED` is written. All of it commits or none of it does. The next
`POST /decisions/evaluate` uses the new version; decisions already stored keep theirs.
Publishes of one policy are serialized by a lock, so the policy never has two active
versions. If the version cannot be published, nothing of the action is kept and the
request stays open at the last step: `409 POLICY_VERSION_SUPERSEDED` when a newer
version is already active (reject the request instead; a rollback is a new version
cloned from the good one), or `409 POLICY_NOT_PUBLISHABLE` when the snapshot no longer
compiles.

The request row is locked for the action, so concurrent approvals are decided one after
the other: the quorum and each transition happen exactly once, and a unique index refuses
a second action of one approver even when two arrive at once. The response is the
request after the action.

Contract for the endpoints implemented so far (RF-001 to RF-020, plus M1 hardening).

- All `/api/v1` endpoints except login require `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.
- Authorization is permission-based. Each operation lists the required permission
  in `x-required-permission`; when `x-alternative-permissions` is also present, holding
  any one of those permissions grants access too. The role-to-permission matrix lives in
  `app/modules/identity/domain/permission.go`.
- Every response produced by the application carries an `X-Request-ID` header, and JSON
  error bodies repeat it as `request_id`. `408` and `413` are written by the HTTP driver
  and may not carry it.
- Semantic validation errors use HTTP 422 consistently.
- Request bodies are limited to 64 KiB. Requests are limited to 3 seconds.
- Optional gateway headers `X-App`, `X-Path-Gateway`, `X-Request-From`, `X-Request-User`,
  `X-Device-ID`, and `X-Request-Tags` are recorded in the server's activity log for tracing.
  They never affect authorization; `X-Request-User` is informational only.
- `408 Request Timeout` and `413 Payload Too Large` are written by the HTTP driver, so
  their body is plain text, not the JSON error envelope. A 408 means the client stopped
  waiting; the handler may still finish server-side, but its database work uses the
  request deadline and is cancelled.
  Unmatched routes (any method) return a JSON `404 ROUTE_NOT_FOUND`.
